statements: The chief problem is recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia in a 19-year-old woman.
Her symptoms progressed from lightheadedness and weakness to repeated episodes of unresponsiveness.
Her symptom pattern is classic for neuroglycopenia and adrenergic activation.
Her symptoms included diaphoresis, palpitations, confusion, weakness, and altered mental status.
Her documented glucose values were 53 mg/dL at home, 60 mg/dL in the ED, 46 mg/dL prehospital, and as low as 23 mg/dL on the third visit.
This fulfills Whipple-type concern.
The Whipple-type concern includes symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia.
The Whipple-type concern includes low measured glucose.
The Whipple-type concern includes improvement after dextrose or food.
Salient positive findings strongly indicate endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
During recurrent hypoglycemia she had markedly elevated insulin levels.
Her free insulin level was 370 mIU/L.
Her total insulin level was 377 mIU/L.
She had elevated C-peptide.
Her C-peptide level was 9.9 ng/mL.
Elevated C-peptide means the insulin is being secreted endogenously or stimulated endogenously rather than being purely injected exogenous insulin.
The hypoglycemia was persistent and severe enough to recur despite repeated D50W boluses and escalating dextrose infusions.
This is compatible with ongoing insulin effect.
Hemoglobin A1C was 5.1%.
There is no evidence of chronic hyperglycemia or known diabetes.
Routine labs were otherwise normal.
Routine hematologic panels were normal.
Routine renal panels were normal.
Routine electrolyte panels were normal.
These normal routine labs argue against organ failure as the cause.
The drug screen was negative.
Standard drug screens do not typically detect sulfonylureas.
Abdominal CT showed no pancreatic mass.
CT can miss small insulinomas.
There is no evidence provided for sepsis.
There is no evidence provided for liver failure.
There is no evidence provided for renal failure.
There is no evidence provided for adrenal crisis.
There is no evidence provided for malnutrition.
There is no evidence provided for pregnancy-related illness.
There is no evidence provided for alcohol intoxication.
There is no evidence provided for drug intoxication.
Vitals were not suggestive of shock.
Vitals were not suggestive of severe infection.
Temperature was normal.
Chemistry panels were otherwise unremarkable.
Head CT was normal.
Normal head CT makes intracranial pathology an unlikely explanation for the altered mental status.
The combination of high insulin plus high C-peptide essentially rules out non-insulin-mediated causes of hypoglycemia.
The combination of high insulin plus high C-peptide argues against exogenous insulin administration.
Exogenous insulin would suppress C-peptide.

The main candidate differentials are sulfonylurea or meglitinide ingestion causing factitious or endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, insulinoma, and less likely surreptitious exogenous insulin use.
Sulfonylurea ingestion fits very well.
Sulfonylurea ingestion causes profound recurrent hypoglycemia with both elevated insulin and elevated C-peptide.
Sulfonylurea ingestion often occurs with normal routine labs and no pancreatic lesion on imaging.
The patient is young.
The patient has psychosocial distress.
These features raise concern for possible factitious or accidental ingestion.
The diagnosis should rest on the biochemical pattern rather than speculation.
Insulinoma is also plausible.
Insulinoma causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia with elevated insulin and C-peptide.
Her age is young for insulinoma.
Abdominal CT showed no pancreatic mass.
The dramatic recurrent episodes over multiple ED visits without a visible lesion make medication-induced hypoglycemia at least more immediately compelling.
Exogenous insulin use is less likely.
The decisive feature is severe hypoglycemia with simultaneously very high insulin and high C-peptide.
This occurred in the setting of otherwise normal labs and a negative standard drug screen.
This biochemical profile is most characteristic of sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia can mimic insulinoma.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia would not be detected on a routine drug screen.
Although insulinoma remains an important alternative, the most likely diagnosis from the provided data is factitious sulfonylurea ingestion causing endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
The differential diagnosis includes sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is high on the differential.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with recurrent severe hypoglycemia.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with markedly elevated insulin.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with elevated C-peptide.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with normal routine labs.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with a negative standard drug screen.
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is associated with no pancreatic mass on CT.
The differential diagnosis includes insulinoma.
Insulinoma is medium on the differential.
The differential diagnosis includes exogenous insulin administration.
Exogenous insulin administration is low on the differential.
The final diagnosis is sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.
